article_title: Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal
citation: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026
title: C-TAM-TPB: Combined Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behavior
description: The C-TAM-TPB framework combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explain technology acceptance through five determinants: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and attitude. These predict behavioral intention, which in turn predicts self-reported frequency of use and observed use. The article states that "This combined model incorporates the five determinants" and applies it per user type to explain portal acceptance among teachers.
requirements: Questionnaire measurement of all five determinants plus behavioral intention and self-reported frequency of use
constraints: Developed for voluntary-use settings; the article notes that findings may differ from business settings because educational institutions serve different goals and teachers have autonomy in technology choice
target_learners: Teachers in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting teachers' acceptance and use of educational technology
examples: Applied to explain KlasCement portal acceptance among 919 Flemish and Dutch teachers
key_sources: Pynoo, B., Tondeur, J., Van Braak, J., Duyck, W., Sijnave, B. & Duyck, P. (2012). Teachers' acceptance and use of an educational portal. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1308-1317. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.026

article_title: Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up?
citation: Laverty Robert B., Chesnut Charles H., Karam Joseph R., L'Huillier Joseph C., Bonte Alexander, Clanahan Julie M., Park Jisuk, Yoon Brian, Krell Robert W. (2025). Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up? Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12150-0
title: C-SATS crowd-sourced video assessment platform with GEARS rubric
description: C-SATS is a commercial, Seattle-based platform that acquires secure operating-room video and performs blinded skill assessments using the Global Evaluative Assessment of Robotic Skills (GEARS) rubric, which "assesses 6 separate domains—depth perception, bimanual dexterity, efficiency, autonomy, force sensitivity, and robotic control" on a 5-point scale with performance anchors at 1, 3, and 5, averaged across evaluators. Its methodology of training non-expert medical personnel as reviewers has been validated in other settings. In this study it was used to score 70 RAC and RIHR videos from 48 surgeons.
requirements: Blinded reviewers not known to participating surgeons, and reviewer training in the GEARS methodology
constraints: The platform could not disclose its inter-rater reliability data, reporting only that all values were greater than 0.9
target_learning_goals: Assessment of robotic surgical technical skill and proficiency for training and credentialing
examples: 48 surgeons submitted 70 videos of RAC and/or RIHR for blinded GEARS review on the platform
key_sources: Laverty Robert B., Chesnut Charles H., Karam Joseph R., L'Huillier Joseph C., Bonte Alexander, Clanahan Julie M., Park Jisuk, Yoon Brian, Krell Robert W. (2025). Evaluating the evaluators: does C-SATS measure up? Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12150-0
